doc.title: Howie Shear interviewed by Monk Rowe, Dunkirk, New York, October 11, 2014

title: Studio work shrinking as synthesizers take over
summary: Shear aspired to studio trumpet and composing; with technology, fewer real instruments are used, mostly synthesized trumpets on TV themes and films.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Good. Well what did you — I’m trying to think how to phrase this question — right now, in 2014, are you doing, in the music business, what you aspired to when you were here?

In 2014? No. No. I was some — when I first got out of school, when I moved to Los Angeles. There was a lot of work and what I really aspired to do was play in the studios as a trumpet player. And there was still quite a bit of work back then. And I always wanted to compose and orchestrate and I did a lot of that. There was a lot of work. So I wasn’t really teaching a lot, although I did teach privately, I didn’t teach in many of the schools yet. But as the technology got better and life went on, there was less and less and less, oh, real instruments playing in the studios. Instead of four trumpets on our date, there was maybe one, maybe two, but one and sometimes none.
Well let me ask about that. Is that because the parts were being overdubbed with synthesizer trumpets or were they just two guys playing, record them twice or all that kind of stuff?

Both that. I still get called to do four parts. But yeah, most of the time it’s synthesized trumpets. You get TV themes. Not movies really, but a lot of TV themes that have trumpets on it and they’re very synthesized. So there’s no trumpets on those. And the movies you do hear that. There’s really ten percent of the epic movies, the big movies like the remix of Robin Hood where they need a hundred piece orchestra, where you have trumpets. But that’s about ten percent. The other 90 percent of the films in Los Angeles are done in the home studios. And I myself have done four scores to films. And one film they gave me a live orchestra. The other three films I had to record it in a midi studio. So I paid people out of my own pocket to come in and sort of like I had a live cellist so it made the other strings sound more real. Or I would put a trumpet over it and maybe synthesized sounds sound more real, and I’ve got a French horn player or maybe one oboe player. So I hire several musicians to make the synthesized sounds sound a little more real. But that’s most of what’s going on.
